statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell and Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017).
plain: After MDMA, some young people have been treated in hospital because the salt (sodium) in their blood fell too low, causing fits and swelling of the brain. It started within hours of taking MDMA. In a UK group of 17 people aged 15 to 26, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid, and two died: both had taken one tablet, had been drinking a lot of water, and drank or were given more water after they felt ill. In California, 73 of 188 people who had their sodium measured had a low level, and 4 of them died. These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens. Most of the UK group had taken one or two tablets, and no study has compared amounts. The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water; that part is not proven.
population: Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and more than 25 published case reports as described in a narrative review
exposure: MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
comparator: None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital
magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, last paragraph (p. 434, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Retrospective series. All documented telephone enquiries to the London centre of the UK National Poisons Information Service from December 1993 to November 1995 were screened for MDMA use complicated by serum sodium below 130 mmol/l, advice cases to March 1996 were added, and a further fatal case was included. Of a mean 13 762 enquiries a month, 135 (1.0%) concerned ecstasy; over the 28-month study period 17 cases were identified (0.4% of all enquiries about ecstasy, a share of telephone calls and not a risk): seven male and 10 female, aged 15 to 26. Table 1 covers the 15 who recovered. Analytical confirmation of MDMA ingestion was obtained in eight cases. Eight patients were known to have ingested a large amount of non-alcoholic or alcoholic fluid; for five the history of fluid ingestion was not available. The pattern was uniform: vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness, agitation and, in 10 patients, seizures; drowsiness, a mute state and disorientation lasted up to 3 days; clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the fall in sodium; in six patients blood and urine tests were consistent with inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). In the two who died, symptoms of cerebral oedema began within 5 hours of one tablet, and in both an excessive amount of fluid had been drunk.

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows 1 to 15 (the table prints rotated; pp. 432-433)
evidence.extracted: The 15 who recovered. Day 1 serum sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l (lowest 107, highest 128). Amount of MDMA stated for 13: half a tablet (2 patients), 1 tablet (5), 1.25 (1), 1.5 (2), 2 (2), 3 (1); amount unknown for 2. Fluids recorded: beer (3 to 4 pints in one patient, 7 pints in another), soft drinks or water described as an excessive amount in several (13 bottles? in one), wine, lager and gin. Temperature at presentation recorded as normal in 12, 37.5 degrees Celsius in 2 and 34.8 in 1. Seizures (grand mal or tonic) in 10. Outcome: complete recovery recorded for 13; pneumonia with difficulty concentrating at 2 months, and aspiration pneumonia needing a tracheostomy, in one patient each. Editors' count: 12 of the 13 patients with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets; 12 of the 15 had a temperature recorded as normal.

The two deaths, both female and both having taken MDMA before. Patient 1, 15 years: one tablet at midnight; dancing, talking and drinking water (at least 3 litres) in rotation; ill and vomiting at 05.00 and given a considerable amount of water; on arrival GCS 3/15 and temperature 32.6 degrees Celsius; serum sodium 125 mmol/l at 12.00 after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid in transport and 1 litre of 0.9% saline; diffuse cerebral oedema with herniation; brain dead on day 2; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/l. Patient 2, 18 years: one tablet at 19.45; talking, smoking cannabis, some alcohol, water from 22.00; ill at 00.15 and drank 6 to 7 cups of water, then vomiting, severe headache, loss of vision and rigidity; temperature 33 degrees; serum sodium 126 mmol/l; marked cerebral oedema; brain dead on day 3; blood MDMA 0.209 mg/l, MDA 0.029 mg/l, ethanol 0.8 g/l. The table's footnote says tablets of ecstasy usually contain 50 to 150 mg MDMA.

The authors write that acute complications after MDMA may be under-reported but are relatively uncommon; that low sodium appears to be a result of water consumption in excess of the body's requirements, compounded by failure of the renal response to water loading; that all patients developed symptoms within 12 hours of taking the drug; and that the nervous-system signs were probably caused by a rapid fall in serum osmolar pressure with movement of water into cells and cerebral oedema, which post-mortem findings confirmed in the two patients who died.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (starts p. 434, right column; ends p. 435, below Table 2)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the low sodium appears to involve inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): in one earlier case plasma arginine vasopressin was inappropriately raised 9 hours after ingestion, and a recent report (not read here) showed a rapid rise in arginine vasopressin after MDMA in eight normally hydrated healthy male volunteers. They add that the mechanism by which MDMA causes this secretion remains to be established, and that acute stress and excessive visual and sound stimuli might contribute, as might nicotine (whether the patients smoked is not known).

evidence.locator: Discussion, the paragraph on early public messages about fluid (p. 436, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say that people who took MDMA were at first advised in underground magazines and the lay press to drink plenty of fluids, a message aimed at preventing collapse from overheating; that this did not say a high fluid intake could be harmful without prolonged exertion; and that it was later put right, especially after the publicity about the fatal cases.

evidence.locator: Methods > Methods of Measurement (p. 166, left column); Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results > Characteristics of Study Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 166, right column)
evidence.extracted: California Poison Control System records. 883 cases were excluded (267 treated at home and others), 5 more as miscoded and 3 with no sex recorded, leaving 545. Sodium values were recorded as given by telephone from the referring hospitals and not checked against medical records. Urine screening was documented in 103 of the 188 (54.8%) with a sodium: sixty-eight (66%) positive and 35 (34%) negative for amphetamines or derivatives; the 35 were still counted as MDMA intoxication on the history given. Of the low-sodium cases, 43 (58.9%) had urine screens. Sodium was documented in 188 (34.5%), with an exact value in 134 (71%) and 'normal' in the rest, similarly in women (105; 35%) and men (83; 33%). Among all 545: tachycardia 43%, agitation 32%, seizures 11%, intensive care one hundred fifty-three (28%), 13 deaths (2.4%). 'Rave party' was the site of ingestion for 50 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 (4.1%) cases of low sodium. The paper reports no fluid-intake figures and no amount of MDMA (editors' reading of the full text).

evidence.locator: Table 1 and Table 2; Results, paragraph on low sodium among the 188 (starts p. 166, right column; ends p. 167, left column)
evidence.extracted: Table 1 (all 545): hyperthermia 40 (7.34%), coma 54 (9.91%), seizure 61 (11.2%), intensive care 153 (28.1%), death 13 (2.4%); mean age 21.2 (SD 6.8), the same in women and men. Among the 188 with a sodium, Table 2 gives low sodium in 55 women and 18 men; median sodium in the low-sodium group 122 mmol/L (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124). Editors' note: 55 plus 18 is 73, as in the abstract, while the last Results paragraph on p. 166 gives 74 (39.4%).

evidence.locator: Table 3; Results, paragraph on fatalities (p. 168, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Table 3, odds ratios of each outcome with low sodium against without, within sex (women 55 of 105; men 18 of 83): hyperthermia 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97); seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); tachycardia 0.33 (0.14 to 0.81) and 0.13 (0.04 to 0.51); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). There were 13 deaths in the 545; 4 were in the low-sodium group (3 women, 1 man), all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines; 2 had seizures, 1 arrived with a temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius and 2 had fluid in the lungs. Of the 9 deaths without low sodium (6 women, 3 men), 3 had hyperthermia.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st to 4th paragraphs (starts p. 168, right column; ends p. 169, right column)
evidence.extracted: Poison-centre data are passive reporting, subject to reporting bias. The authors say they may have missed cases and underestimated complications; that referral bias may produce spectrum bias, the series representing the more severe outcomes and possibly overestimating how often low sodium and poor outcomes occur; that exposure rests on a history from the patient or a witness and may include other substances sold as ecstasy; that laboratory confirmation of MDMA was lacking in a significant share and no gas chromatography with mass spectrometry was reported; that no sodium was recorded in 65.5% of cases, the timing of the sodium was not consistent, and low sodium may be relatively benign and self-correcting in some; and that differing body build, kidney function, hydration, coingestions and behaviour limit conclusions about how likely a given population is to develop low sodium.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 1855, right column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: symptomatic low sodium (usually below 130 mEq/L) was first described by Maxwell and colleagues in 1993 and more than 25 separate case reports have been published since; sodium on presentation ranged from 101 to 130 mEq/L, and the vast majority of cases were in females aged 15 to 30 who took a single dose of ecstasy. The review attributes excess water intake in part to a harmful response to overheating (chill-out areas with free or cheap water or low-solute drinks), together with amphetamine-induced dry mouth and thirst; whether ecstasy gives a primary drive to drink is not known but has been hypothesized. Editors' count of Table 3: 32 published cases, 27 labelled F, 1 W and 4 M, 16 deaths, 15 recoveries and 1 not available; 10 rows are taken from the California series (reference 82 in the review).

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 2nd paragraph, the case report (starts p. 1855, right column; continues p. 1856, left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: an 18-year-old woman came to an emergency department soon after taking five tablets of ecstasy, with severe headache and thirst and a serum sodium of 136 mEq/L; she then drank 1700 ml of water, her headache worsened and the repeat sodium was 130 mEq/L, with urine osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 101 mEq/L and plasma arginine vasopressin 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6). The review reasons that ready fluids, severe thirst and advice to drink copiously are likely not enough on their own, because the kidney can usually excrete free water faster than it is taken in, so the kidney's water excretion must also be impaired, as the raised urine osmolality and vasopressin in this and other cases suggest.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, paragraphs on vasopressin secretion and on sweat sodium (p. 1856, left and right columns)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: MDMA has been shown in case reports and controlled settings to induce vasopressin secretion. Henry and colleagues gave 40 mg (against a common street dose of 100 mg) to eight healthy volunteers and found vasopressin rose within 1 to 2 hours (from a baseline range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L to 2.46 to 9.16) with a slight fall in serum sodium; several other controlled studies are said to show a rise within 1 to 2 hours, and the rise is said to correlate negatively with MDMA levels, suggesting a metabolite. Sweat sodium loss is judged likely marginal, the majority of case reports lack significant hyperthermia, and the review concludes that increased water ingestion with urinary water retention is the main driving force. None of these primary studies was read here.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: Hyponatraemia, which the authors describe as frequently observed in ecstasy intoxications, was not assessed in the controlled laboratory sessions of 166 volunteers, so blood sodium was not measured there.

risk_of_bias.note: Both series are ROBINS-I critical on their cards: cases are those that were reported to a poison service, exposure is by history (MDMA confirmed in only part), sodium was recorded in about a third of the Californian cases, and values were given by telephone. One level, not two, because the claim describes what was seen in these cases and gives no rate.

inconsistency.note: The UK and Californian series, from different countries, years and services, agree on the pattern (young people, within hours, seizures and brain swelling). They differ in the share of women (10 of 17 against 55 of 73 low-sodium cases), which the claim leaves to the separate claim on who is affected.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who came to a poison service or hospital, with the limits stated.

imprecision.note: Small counts (2 deaths in 17; 4 in 73), no intervals for any share, and an internal inconsistency in the Californian count of low-sodium cases (73 and 74).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the published case reports are selected by nature, and the claim takes no figure from them.

grade.reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.

verification.flag_note: Rests on two case series and one narrative review (METHODS 6.3 and 12), so it stays draft. A 2016 controlled study in healthy volunteers (Baggott et al., doi 10.1155/2016/2175896; seen only as a PMC abstract, not read, no reference record here) reports that a water load lowered sodium more after MDMA than after placebo while vasopressin and copeptin did not rise; if confirmed, the vasopressin explanation these papers give would be contested and the mechanism sentence should be revisited. The primary vasopressin papers (Henry 1998, Forsling and Fallon 2001-2002, Wolff 2006) and the case reports (Brvar 2004, Budisavljevic 2003) have no reference record here and were not read. The first UK death appears to be the Australian fatal case the UK authors include from an earlier report (Parr 1997); the review lists a 15-year-old female with sodium 125 who died. The UK abstract gives 14 complete recoveries and 11 with seizures (15 and 17 patients); Table 1 labels 13 of the 15 survivors as complete recovery.
